content: The broad ligament of the uterus is a wide fold of peritoneum that connects the sides of the uterus to the walls and floor of the pelvis. Despite its name, the term ligament is somewhat misleading, as ligaments typically refer to structures that connect bones to one another. The broad ligament contains several important anatomical structures, including the fallopian tubes, the ovarian artery, the uterine artery, the ovary, the ovarian ligament, and the round ligament of the uterus. The broad ligament can be divided into three distinct subcomponents: 1. Mesometrium: This is the mesentery of the uterus and constitutes the largest portion of the broad ligament. 2. Mesosalpinx: This part surrounds the uterine (fallopian) tube. 3. Mesovarium: This part surrounds the ovary. Some sources consider the suspensory ligament of the ovary to be part of the broad ligament, while others regard it as a termination of the ligament. Structurally, the peritoneum surrounding the uterus resembles a flat sheet that folds over the uterus. On the sides of the uterus, this sheet comes into direct contact with itself, forming the double layer of peritoneum known as the broad ligament. The free edge of the broad ligament contains the uterine tubes running between its two layers, and this specific region is referred to as the mesosalpinx. Functionally, the broad ligament acts as a mesentery for the uterus, ovaries, and uterine tubes. It plays a crucial role in maintaining the uterus in its proper anatomical position.
